intro.title: for loops
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A `for` loop runs the same code once for each value of a vector. The loop variable takes each value in turn:

```
crops <- c("kale", "beans", "mint")
for (crop in crops) {
  cat("Water the", crop, "\n")
}
```

A very common pattern is a **running total**: start with 0 before the loop, and add to it each time round:

```
rain <- c(2.4, 0, 5.1, 1.2)
total <- 0
for (mm in rain) {
  total <- total + mm
}
total    # 8.7
```

When you need the position as well as the value, loop over `seq_along(x)`, which gives 1, 2, 3, … up to the length. Then `x[i]` is the value and `i` its position:

```
days <- c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed")
for (i in seq_along(days)) {
  cat(i, days[i], "\n")
}
```

To collect a result per value, make an empty vector first and fill it in: `out <- numeric(length(x))`, then `out[i] <- …` inside the loop.

Many loops in R can be replaced by vector maths: `sum(rain)` is the same as the running total above, and shorter. Loops shine when each step depends on the one before, or when you are doing something (printing, reading files) rather than calculating.

intro.title: while loops
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A `for` loop runs a known number of times. A `while` loop keeps going **as long as** a condition is TRUE, which suits questions like "how many weeks until I have saved 500?":

```
saved <- 0
weeks <- 0
while (saved < 500) {
  saved <- saved + 45
  weeks <- weeks + 1
}
weeks    # 12
```

Each time round, R checks the condition first. When it becomes FALSE, the loop stops and the code after it runs.

Something inside the loop **must** change the condition, or it runs forever. If your code seems stuck, that's usually why: press **Stop** to end it.

Two keywords control any loop. `break` stops the loop straight away. `next` skips the rest of this time round and goes on to the next:

```
for (t in c(22, NA, 27, 31)) {
  if (is.na(t)) next          # skip missing readings
  if (t > 30) break           # stop at the first very hot one
  cat(t, "\n")
}
```

intro.title: Writing functions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
When you find yourself writing the same calculation again and again, make it a **function** of your own. You save it in a name, like any value, with `function()`:

```
ride_cost <- function(minutes) {
  1 + 0.15 * minutes
}
ride_cost(47)    # 8.05
ride_cost(12)    # 2.8
```

`minutes` is the function's **argument**: a name for whatever value it is called with. The code in the braces is the **body**. The value of the last line is what the function gives back, its **return value**, so `ride_cost(47)` is 8.05.

A function works like R's own ones: on vectors (`ride_cost(c(12, 47))` gives both costs), inside other calls (`round(ride_cost(47))`), and in new columns (`trips$cost <- ride_cost(trips$minutes)`).

Variables made inside a function stay inside it. If the body says `total <- …`, that `total` disappears when the function finishes and doesn't touch a `total` outside. Only the return value comes out.

Good functions do one clear job and have a name that says what it is, usually a verb or a noun for the result: `ride_cost`, `to_fahrenheit`, `tidy_name`.

intro.title: Arguments and defaults
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A function can take several arguments, separated by commas. When you call it, the values are matched by position, or by name:

```
ride_cost <- function(minutes, rate) {
  1 + rate * minutes
}
ride_cost(47, 0.15)
ride_cost(rate = 0.15, minutes = 47)   # the same
```

Give an argument a **default** with `=` in the definition. Callers can then leave it out, and only give it when they want something different:

```
ride_cost <- function(minutes, rate = 0.15, unlock = 1) {
  unlock + rate * minutes
}
ride_cost(47)                  # 8.05
ride_cost(47, unlock = 0)      # 7.05: members unlock free
```

Put the arguments everyone needs first, without defaults, and the optional ones after, with sensible defaults. Name the optional ones when you call the function, as above: `unlock = 0` is much clearer than a bare 0 in third place.

R's own functions work exactly this way: `round(x, digits = 0)`, `mean(x, na.rm = FALSE)`, `paste(…, sep = " ")`. Now you can read their help pages: the usage line shows every argument and its default.

intro.title: sapply and lapply
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Many functions already work on whole vectors. When one doesn't (because it uses `if`, say, which needs a single value), `sapply()` runs it once for each value and collects the answers in a vector, with no loop to write:

```
grade <- function(score) if (score >= 50) "pass" else "fail"
sapply(c(71, 44, 88), grade)    # "pass" "fail" "pass"
```

`sapply(x, f)` is the same as a `for` loop that fills a vector with `f(x[i])`, just shorter. Extra arguments go after the function: `sapply(lists, mean, na.rm = TRUE)`.

For a quick one-off, write the function right inside the call. R has a short way to write a small function: `\(x) x * 2` means `function(x) x * 2`.

```
sapply(c("kale", "beans"), \(w) paste0(toupper(substr(w, 1, 1)), substr(w, 2, nchar(w))))
```

`lapply()` does the same but always gives a **list**, one item per value. Use it when each answer is more than one value, or when you want to keep them separate. `sapply()` simplifies to a vector or table when it can.

They also work over lists and over the columns of a data frame, because a data frame is a list of columns: `sapply(df, class)` gives every column's type in one line. The next stage uses that a lot.

intro.title: Functions for data frames
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Your own functions really pay off with data frames, where the same steps are needed for many columns or many tables.

A data frame is a list of columns, so `sapply()` runs a function on every column. That gives a one-line overview of a whole table:

```
class_results <- data.frame(
  student = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal", "Ivy", "Jo", "Kai", "Lea"),
  group = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"),
  test1 = c(72, 65, 88, 54, 91, 47, 76, 69, 83, 58, 64, 95),
  test2 = c(78, 70, 85, 61, 94, NA, 80, 66, 88, 62, 71, 97)
)
```

```
sapply(class_results, class)                     # every column's type
sapply(class_results, \(col) sum(is.na(col)))    # NAs per column
sapply(class_results[, c("test1", "test2")], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

A function can take a whole data frame as its argument and give back a number, a vector or a new data frame. That's how you package up a cleaning step or a report so it can be used on next week's data too:

```
pass_rate <- function(df, column, pass = 50) {
  round(mean(df[[column]] >= pass, na.rm = TRUE) * 100)
}
pass_rate(class_results, "test1")
pass_rate(class_results, "test2", pass = 60)
```

Note `df[[column]]`: the column name arrives as text in a variable, so `$` won't work (`df$column` would look for a column literally called "column").

Your functions also work as the `FUN` of `tapply()` and `aggregate()`, so any summary you can write, you can get per group.

readings <- data.frame(
  sensor = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C"),
  temp = c(21.4, NA, 22.0, 85.0, 21.8, -40),
  humidity = c(55, 61, NA, 58, 140, 52)

check_table <- function(df, limits) {

report <- function(df, limits) {

    x <- df[[col]]
    low <- limits[[col]][1]
    high <- limits[[col]][2]

    n_out <- sum(x < low | x > high, na.rm = TRUE)
